title: Not Angles but angels
hookLine: the story goes Gregory saw English boys in a market, and later sent Augustine of Canterbury (597)

cards: A market in Rome. Merchants have arrived with goods to sell, and among the goods, the story says, are boys: fair-skinned, light-haired, good-looking. A Roman monk stops and stares.
He asks where they're from. Britain, he's told. Are they Christians?
No. He sighs, and asks the name of their people. Angles, they tell him.
And the monk, who is Gregory, before he became pope, says something people have retold ever since.

teach.b: The story comes from Bede, an English monk who wrote a history of the Church among his own people. He's careful to say it was handed down from those before him.

In Bede's telling, Gregory answers: good, for they have the faces of angels, and such people ought to share heaven with the angels. The neat phrase, not Angles but angels, is how later people shortened it.
Bede has Gregory keep going. Their region is called Deira; Gregory turns that into the Latin for from wrath: they'll be rescued from wrath. Their king is Ælle.
Then, says Gregory, Alleluia must be sung there. Three puns in a row. Next, what he did.
Bede says Gregory asked to go to Britain himself, but the people of Rome wouldn't let him leave. Later, as pope, he sent others: a monk named Augustine and a band of monks.
Not the Augustine of the Confessions; this is Augustine of Canterbury. Now the wobble.
Bede says that partway there, the monks lost their nerve. They'd heard the people were fierce, and they didn't know the language. They sent Augustine back to ask Gregory to call it off.
Gregory wrote back and told them to go on. And the landing. Bede says they came to the king of Kent, whose wife was already a Christian.
The king met them outdoors, worried about magic indoors.
They came carrying a silver cross and a picture of Christ painted on a board, singing as they walked. The king let them stay and preach, and gave them a place in Canterbury.
That's the mission to the English: a pun in a market, and a group of frightened monks who kept going.

how: Catholics honor Saint Augustine of Canterbury as the apostle of the English and Saint Gregory the Great as the pope who sent him, and both have feasts on the Church's calendar.

games.q: Not Angles but angels — tap the pairs.

s: Bede records Gregory saying exactly not Angles but angels
Bede has a longer line about angelic faces; the short phrase is a later shortening.
Gregory's monks wanted to turn back before reaching England
Bede says they lost their nerve and sent Augustine to ask to be released.
the Augustine sent to England wrote the Confessions
this is Augustine of Canterbury, a different man.

games.q: you're Gregory. the monks you sent to England have stopped partway and sent Augustine back, afraid of a fierce people whose language they don't know. what do you do?
o: write back and tell them to go on.
games.why: Bede says Gregory wrote telling them to go on, and they reached the king of Kent with a silver cross and a painted image of Christ.

practice: Start with a thread that already reaches you from England: a book, a song, someone who lives there. Follow it to the people at the other end and let them be enough; you don't need to hold a whole country.
If you pray, pray for the people of England, as Gregory did when he sent his monks; if not, let your goodwill travel back along the thread.

wordCard.voice: Augustine. The monk Gregory sent to lead the mission to England, after a pun about angels in a Roman market. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: Angles, angels — the two words Gregory's pun plays on.

carryVoice: Your line: the mission to the english. Gregory's answer to their fear was simple: go on. Day seven hundred fifty-five, done.
